blocks.c: Three: The Second Register

The Medical Officer of Health for the county produced an annual report every year from 1875, and the county archive holds a complete run, and on the fifth of June Ilse Vanterpool drove eleven miles down the valley and forty miles across the county to read the one for 1942.

She had worked in that building for fourteen years. It was extremely strange to walk into her own searchroom as a reader, and to sign the register, and to be brought a volume by a young man called Delaney who had been her trainee two years before and who had the decency to say nothing at all except "You're brown."
"I'm outdoors."
"Suits you. There's a rumour you've gone native and live in a caravan."
"I do live in a caravan."
"Right," said Delaney. "Well. Table four."
What the doctor wrote
The Medical Officer's report for 1942 devotes a page and a half to diphtheria, which was the great enemy of that decade and which the whole apparatus of public health had by then been trained on.

Diphtheria. There were in the year 61 notified cases in the county, with 4 deaths, a case fatality of 6.5 per cent, continuing the decline noted in previous years and attributable in large measure to the immunisation campaign and to the prompt administration of antitoxin.

An outbreak occurred at Hallowmere in February, following the admission of a case at the school. Six cases were notified. Three deaths occurred. The outbreak was contained by closure of the school and by immunisation of the remaining children of the parish, of whom 61 were immunised in the week of 16 February.
Three deaths.
Ilse read it four times and then sat back and looked at the ceiling of a searchroom she had worked in for fourteen years.

The county's Medical Officer, a man whose entire professional function was to count diseases accurately and who would have had the notification cards on his desk within a day, recorded three deaths at Hallowmere in February 1942.
The parish register recorded five burials.

She copied both, exactly, with references. She ordered up the registrar's indexes and established that death certificates existed for three children in the Hallowmere sub-district in February 1942 — Rhys, Pike, Callow — and none for anyone named Braith, in that quarter or in any quarter that year, anywhere in the county.
Then she ordered up the newspaper.
The Gazette

The county Gazette for the twenty-seventh of February 1942 has eleven column inches on the outbreak, under a headline that would not be permitted now, and it is the only account written at the time by anybody who was not in the village.

The sympathy of the whole district will go out to the parents of Hallowmere, where three children have died in an outbreak of diphtheria at the village school. Dr. Marris, the Medical Officer, told our reporter that the outbreak had been contained with commendable speed and that the co-operation of the villagers had been exemplary. The school reopened on Monday.

A further sadness attaches to the deaths of two evacuated children of the parish, brother and sister, who were among those affected. Their mother was killed in the raid on Ferrisport in August 1940 and no other relative has been traced. The Rector, the Rev. T. J. Ammons, conducted the funerals.
There it was, in print, in a newspaper of record: five children, two of them evacuees, brother and sister, no relatives, funerals conducted.
And in the Medical Officer's report, three.
Ilse sat with both open in front of her and did the thing she was best at in the world, which was to stop wanting an answer and ask instead who each document was for.

The Medical Officer's report is an internal, statutory, numerical document produced from notification cards for the purpose of measuring disease. Nobody reads it. It has no audience and therefore no reason to lie.
The newspaper is written from what the village tells the reporter.
The parish register is written by the rector.

Which meant that the falsehood, if there was one, had been produced in the village and pushed outwards, and had gone out through the two channels the village controlled — its rector and its gossip — and had not gone out through the one channel it did not control, which was a doctor with a card index.
She wrote in her notebook:
The village told the outside world that five children died. The public health apparatus, which counts independently, recorded three. Two children were therefore removed from the world on paper only.

This was not done by an individual. A rector wrote a register entry, a schoolmistress made a log entry, a sexton did not dig two graves and did not charge for them, a stonemason cut two stones with initials and no names, a newspaper was told a story, and everyone in a village of two hundred and forty people knew and no one contradicted it for fifty-two years.
I have been thinking of this as a falsification. It is not a falsification. It is a decision.
Enid Sowerby

She found the schoolmistress's assistant on the eleventh of June, and she found her the way archivists find people, which is by not looking for a person at all but for a document with a person's name on it.

The school log book named an assistant teacher, Miss E. Bowen, appointed in 1938. The county's education committee minutes recorded a Miss E. Bowen resigning her post in 1946 on her marriage — women had to, then — to a Mr. Sowerby. The county's electoral registers had a Mrs. E. Sowerby in the town from 1946 to 1981, and after 1981 nothing, which usually means death and sometimes means a home.

It meant a home. Ashecroft, on the north road, and Mrs. Enid Sowerby was ninety-five, and the matron said she had very good days and very bad days, and that on a good day she would talk your ear off, and that Ilse should come on a Tuesday morning because Tuesday morning was hair.
She was in a chair by a window with a rug over her knees, small and upright, with her hair freshly set and a cardigan the colour of a robin's egg.
"You're from the county," she said. "They said the county. Are you here about the school?"
"I'm here about Hallowmere, Mrs. Sowerby. I'm making the record before they flood it."
"They're flooding it."
"In October."
"Well," said Mrs. Sowerby, and looked out of the window for a while. "That's a thing I hoped to be dead for."
Ilse said nothing, because there was nothing to say to that, and because she had learned early that the largest single mistake in oral history is filling a silence.
"Sit down, then," said Mrs. Sowerby. "Not there. That's Marjorie's chair and she'll be difficult. What do you want to know?"
"Miss Prosser," said Ilse.
The old woman's whole face changed.
What Miss Prosser was like
"Anwen Prosser was the finest teacher I ever saw and she frightened the life out of me for six years."
"How?"

"She was thirty-four when she came up with those children and she had lost her school and her house and every one of her own papers in the raid and she had walked forty of them onto a bus and up a valley and she was not going to lose a single one of them, and God help anybody who got in the way of that. God help them." Mrs. Sowerby's hands moved on the rug. "She fought the billeting officer. She fought the county. She fought Mr. Wardle at the school over the two shifts and she won, and we went to one shift by November and thirty-nine of us in a room built for twenty-eight, and it was chaos, and it was better."
"Thirty-nine," said Ilse, carefully. "I thought forty-one arrived."
Mrs. Sowerby looked at her.

It was a long look, of a quality Ilse had not had directed at her before: entirely lucid, entirely aware, and calculating. Whatever else the years had taken, they had not taken the thing that assesses a stranger.
"Forty-one arrived," she said. "Yes. That's right. You've read the log book."
"I've read the log book."
"And the admission register."
"Thirty-nine."
"Mm." Mrs. Sowerby put her head back. "Are you going to write down what I say?"
"Yes. That is exactly what I am going to do, and I would rather tell you that than not."
"Good. The last one didn't."
Ilse's pencil stopped.
"The last one?"

"There was a man in about 1979, from a university, doing evacuation. Very keen. He had a machine." She sniffed. "He asked me eleven questions and every one of them was the question he already had the answer to. I gave him nothing and he went away happy."
"What would you have told him," said Ilse, "if he had asked the right one?"
The right question
"Ask it, then," said Mrs. Sowerby. "Go on. You've come forty miles."

Ilse put her pencil down flat on her notebook, which she did to indicate that she was not writing, and which is a small piece of theatre she was not proud of and used perhaps four times in her career.
"Mrs. Sowerby," she said, "in February 1942 three children died in Hallowmere and five were buried. Where did Nell and Tomas Braith go?"
The room was quiet. Down the corridor a trolley went past with cups on it.

"Nowhere," said Enid Sowerby. "That's the answer. They went nowhere at all. They were at the school on the second of March and they were at the school for the whole of the war and Nell Braith took her scholarship in 1943 and went to the grammar in the town on the bus like the rest of them, and Tomas left at fourteen and went to Meddick's farm, and neither of them ever left this valley until they were grown, and the whole of the county knew them and not one soul asked."
"Under what names?"

"Under their own names," said Mrs. Sowerby, "which is the part that nobody has ever understood and which is why your man from the university got nothing. They didn't hide. That is not what was done. What was done was much simpler and much cleverer and it was Anwen Prosser's idea and it was the wickedest thing I have ever been part of and I would do it again this afternoon."
She leaned forward, and her voice did not drop, because she was ninety-five and had stopped bothering with that sort of thing.

"They put the two children who died in the graves under the names of the two who were going to be taken away, and they put the two who lived into the world with the names of the two who died. That is all. Grace Callow's little brother and a boy of the Pikes went into the ground as Nell and Tomas Braith. And Nell and Tomas walked out of that school in March as Marta Rhys and Emrys Pike, and their names were on the register and their names were in the parish and their names were on two headstones in the churchyard so that anyone who ever came looking would find them dead and stop looking."
The reason
"Why?" said Ilse. Her voice sounded ordinary and she was surprised by that. "Mrs. Sowerby. Why?"
"Because of the letter."
"What letter?"

"The letter from the Ferrisport authority in January 1942 that said that as no relative had been traced, the two Braith children were to be transferred at the end of the school term to institutional care, and that a place had been found for the girl at a home in the west of the county and a place had been found for the boy at a training establishment, and would the billeting officer arrange it." Mrs. Sowerby's mouth was a hard line. "Two different places. Four hundred miles between them, or as good as."
"They were going to be separated."

"They were going to be separated, and Anwen Prosser had promised their mother's neighbour on a pavement in Ferrisport in September 1940 that she would keep them together, and there was nothing she could do about it, because the letter was correct. That is what people don't understand about it. The letter was not cruel. The letter was correct. There was no relative, and the billet was temporary, and the authority had a duty, and a girl of eleven and a boy of thirteen were about to be sent to the two places the system had for them and that would have been that."
"So she—"

"So she came to the school on a Thursday morning in February with her coat still on and she said, Enid, there are two children dead in this village this week and they are going to be buried anyway. And I said, Anwen, whatever it is you're about to say, don't say it in a school."
Mrs. Sowerby looked out of the window at the car park.

"She said it in the vestry that night," she said, "to the rector and to Aled Stammers and to Mrs. Callow, who had buried her son on the Tuesday, and it was Mrs. Callow who said yes first. That is the thing I have carried for fifty-two years and I would like somebody to write it down properly at last. Not the teacher. Not the rector. The mother. She had put her boy in the ground on the Tuesday and on the Thursday she sat in a cold vestry and said, he can have my Robert's grave and Robert can have his name, and I'll not have another mother's children split up over a form."
What Ilse did with her hands
Ilse Vanterpool sat in a chair in a nursing home on the north road for a while without doing anything at all.

Then she picked up her pencil and wrote, at the top of a clean page, the date, the place, the time, and the words: Mrs. Enid Sowerby (b. Bowen), aged 95, formerly assistant teacher, Hallowmere school, 1938-46. Interview. Present: E. Sowerby, I. Vanterpool. No recording made; notes taken at the time, written up same day.

And then she wrote it all down, for an hour and a quarter, and asked the questions in the order you ask them, and did not once let her hand shake on the page, because there is a discipline for this and she had it and it held.

She established: the date of the vestry meeting (the nineteenth of February, a Thursday). Those present. The disposal of the real Braith records — burned in the vestry grate, which is why the admission register is short and the attendance register is not. The rector's role, which was to write the entries and to preach a sermon the following Sunday on the subject of Rahab and the spies, which Mrs. Sowerby said nobody in that church ever forgot.
And the fate, afterwards, of the two children.
Marta Rhys — Nell Braith — had left the valley in 1949, aged eighteen, gone to a city, married in 1953, and never come back, not once, not for any funeral.
Emrys Pike — Tomas Braith — had never left it at all.
"Never?"

"He has been over that hill to market and he has been down to the town for a doctor and he came here once in 1981 to see me because Anwen died and he wanted to hear it from somebody who'd been there." Mrs. Sowerby's hands were quiet on the rug now. "But he has never left, and he cannot leave, and I would think that a woman of your trade would work out why in about four seconds."
Ilse had worked it out in rather less than that.

A man whose name is only good in one parish cannot go anywhere that asks for papers. He can hold land in that name because the land was held by a Pike and the parish knew. He can be on the electoral register because the overseer of the register was a neighbour. He can be paid for honey in cash. He cannot draw a pension, or open an account at a new bank, or take a passport, or marry, or move to a county where nobody remembers 1942, and the whole apparatus of his life is a hand-built thing that only exists inside a valley that was going to be under ninety feet of water in October.
"He'll have to go up to Culverton with everyone else," said Ilse.
"Yes."
"They'll want a name."
Nell
Ilse asked one more question and it was not for the record, and she knew it was not for the record while she was asking it, and she asked it anyway.
"What was she like?"
Mrs. Sowerby did not pretend not to know which she.

"Sharp," she said. "Sharp as a tack and no manners at all when she came, and why would she have any, she was a city child with a dead mother in a valley full of farmers who thought she talked funny. She fought two boys in her first fortnight and won both."
"That doesn't sound like her."

"No. It wouldn't." The old woman's eyes came round, mild and terrible. "She stopped, you see. In March 1942 she stopped. That was the price of it and nobody had thought about the price, because we were all so pleased with ourselves for having found a way. A child who has been told that she is now somebody else, and that the whole village will hold the lie for her, and that if she ever forgets herself in front of a stranger the thing they did in the vestry is undone and everybody who helped goes to prison — that child does not fight boys in the yard any more. That child becomes extremely careful and stays extremely careful for the rest of her life."
Ilse put her hand flat on her notebook.
"She was careful," she said. "She was the most careful person I have ever known. She checked the gas twice. She kept every receipt. She would not have a photograph taken."
"No," agreed Mrs. Sowerby. "She wouldn't."
"I thought it was the war."
"It was the war." A pause. "Just not the part of it you were thinking of."
There was a long silence, and the trolley came back down the corridor the other way, and somewhere a television was on.
"Did she know?" said Ilse. "At eleven. Did she understand what was being done?"

"She understood better than any of us. She was the one who said, in that vestry, that it would only work if they were buried under their own names, because a stranger looking for Nell Braith would want to see Nell Braith in the ground and would not be satisfied by two children who had never existed." Mrs. Sowerby shook her head slowly. "That was an eleven-year-old. That is what a raid and a dead mother and four months of a billeting officer will make of an eleven-year-old, and if you want to know why she never came back to this valley, my dear, it is not because she was ashamed of us. It is because she thought of it, and it worked, and she had to look at those two stones every Sunday for seven years."
"And she never told me."

"No," said Enid Sowerby. "And she never told me either, and I was in the room. She left in 1949 and she wrote to Anwen twice and then she stopped, and Anwen said, quite rightly, that this was the correct behaviour and that we should all be glad of it and that she would not be written to again."
She reached out and put her hand, which was very light, on Ilse's wrist.

"There isn't a name for what you are to me," she said. "But I taught your mother her multiplication and I am extremely pleased to have met you, and now I am going to say the thing I have been working round to for an hour, so pay attention.

"There's a dead girl called Marta Rhys who has your face, my dear, which I noticed when you walked in and which I have been waiting an hour and a half for you to mention. And there's a man of sixty-five in a cottage by a river with a dead boy's name and eleven hives of bees, and in four months the water comes, and I have been lying awake about it since the day the scheme went through."
